analogy.p: Aerobic respiration is like a power station: glucose is the fuel, oxygen lets it burn completely, and the products are exhaust gases (carbon dioxide and water) plus a lot of useful energy. Just as a fire needs oxygen to burn fuel fully and release lots of heat, cells need oxygen to break glucose down fully. Where it breaks down: a power station burns fuel in a single violent reaction, whereas cells release the energy in many small, enzyme-controlled steps so it is captured gradually instead of all wasted as heat.

bullets: Respiration is **continuous**: it happens all day and all night, in all living cells, never stopping while the organism is alive.
It is an **exothermic** reaction: energy is released, and some of it appears as heat (which is why mammals and birds stay warm).

The energy is not 'made': it is **transferred from the chemical energy store of glucose** to a form cells can use (stored temporarily in a molecule called ATP, which you do not need by name for AQA GCSE but is useful to know).
Plants respire as well as photosynthesise. In the light they do both; in the dark they only respire.
Respiration is controlled by **enzymes**, so it is affected by temperature and pH like any enzyme-controlled reaction.
Do not write 'respiration makes energy'. Say 'respiration **transfers** (or releases) energy'.
core.p: **Respiration** is the chemical process that **transfers energy from glucose** (food molecules) so that cells can use it. It is **not** the same as breathing: breathing (ventilation) is just moving air in and out of the lungs. Respiration happens inside **every living cell** of every organism, in plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms. It is an **exothermic reaction**, which means it **transfers energy to the surroundings** (some as heat).

bullets: **Aerobic** = with oxygen. Glucose is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and water.
**Anaerobic** = without oxygen. Glucose is only partly broken down, so far less energy is transferred (see the anaerobic respiration notes).
Aerobic respiration takes place **continuously in plants and animals**.
The prefix 'aero-' means air; 'an-' means without. This is an easy way to remember them.
Aerobic respiration is the type to assume in an exam unless the question says oxygen is lacking, for example during hard exercise.
core.h: Aerobic versus anaerobic: the two types
core.p: Respiration can take place **aerobically** (using **oxygen**) or **anaerobically** (**without oxygen**). **Aerobic respiration** is the main type: it is what happens in your cells most of the time. It requires a good supply of oxygen, which is why we breathe and why blood carries oxygen to every cell. It is the **more efficient** type because glucose is broken down **completely**, so **much more energy** is transferred per glucose molecule.

bullets: **Reactants**: glucose and oxygen.
**Products**: carbon dioxide and water (plus energy transferred).
Glucose comes from digested food (animals) or photosynthesis (plants); oxygen is taken in by breathing or diffusion.
Carbon dioxide is a waste product, removed by the blood to the lungs and breathed out; in plants it diffuses out through the stomata (or is reused for photosynthesis).
Water is produced too, which is why exhaled air is humid and why you can see your breath mist on a cold day.
Energy is a result, not a substance. Never write 'energy' as one of the chemicals that are used up.
core.p: The word equation for aerobic respiration is **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**. You must be able to write it from memory, with the **arrow** showing the direction of change and energy shown as being **transferred** (energy is usually written on the right as a product or above the arrow, depending on the question). The reactants on the left are used up; the products on the right are made.

bullets: Glucose is **C6H12O6**: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen, 6 oxygen atoms.
Left side atoms: C = 6; H = 12; O = 6 + (6 x 2) = 18.
Right side atoms: C = 6 (from 6CO2); H = 6 x 2 = 12 (from 6H2O); O = (6 x 2) + 6 = 12 + 6 = 18. Both sides match, so the equation is balanced.
**One glucose molecule** needs **six oxygen molecules** and produces six carbon dioxide and six water molecules.
Common error: writing O instead of O2. Oxygen gas exists as molecules of **O2**.
Higher tier link: you may be asked a chemistry-style calculation with this equation (see the worked example). The ratio is **1 : 6 : 6 : 6** in moles.
core.p: The balanced symbol equation is **C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O**. A balanced equation has the **same number of each type of atom on both sides**, because atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction (conservation of mass). Checking the balance is a good habit: it also proves you wrote the formulae correctly.

bullets: Mitochondria have a folded inner membrane that gives a large surface area for the enzymes involved.
Muscle cells have lots of mitochondria because contraction needs a lot of energy.
Sperm cells have many mitochondria in the middle section to power the tail for swimming.
Active transport cells (e.g. root hair cells, gut lining) also contain many mitochondria.
Bacteria do not have mitochondria but many still respire aerobically using their cell membrane.
Exam link: 'Why do muscle cells have many mitochondria?' Answer: **they transfer energy by aerobic respiration, which is needed for contraction**.
core.p: In animal and plant cells, most of the reactions in aerobic respiration take place in the **mitochondria** (singular mitochondrion), the tiny structures you learn about in cell biology. The first stage that splits glucose happens in the cytoplasm, but the mitochondria are where **most of the energy is transferred**. Cells that need a lot of energy, such as **muscle cells**, **sperm cells** and **liver cells**, have **many mitochondria**.

bullets: **Building larger molecules from smaller ones**: e.g. making **proteins from amino acids**, **starch from glucose**, **lipids** from fatty acids and glycerol, and **DNA** from nucleotides.
**Movement**: muscles contract using energy transferred from respiration (e.g. in the heart, leg muscles, and in the gut for peristalsis).
**Keeping warm**: mammals and birds use energy from respiration to maintain a constant body temperature, also by shivering (muscle contraction releases heat).
**Active transport**: moving substances against a concentration gradient, such as mineral ions into root hair cells.
**Nerve impulses** and cell division also need energy.
Plants use respiration energy to build sugars into **cellulose**, proteins and so on, and for growth.
core.h: Why living things need the energy
core.p: The energy released by respiration is used for everything an organism does. The specification highlights three uses: **chemical reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones**, **movement**, and **keeping warm** (in mammals and birds, which are warm-blooded). You should be able to give an example of each. Without a steady supply of energy from respiration the cells would stop working and the organism would die.

bullets: Red blood cells carry oxygen as **oxyhaemoglobin**.
Glucose dissolves in blood plasma.
Carbon dioxide leaves cells by **diffusion**, travels in the blood plasma and is exhaled.
Larger organisms need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems because their surface area to volume ratio is small.
During exercise, more oxygen and glucose are needed, so heart rate and breathing rate increase (see response to exercise).
If oxygen supply cannot keep up, cells switch to anaerobic respiration.
core.h: Supply of reactants: how oxygen and glucose reach cells
core.p: For aerobic respiration to continue, cells need a constant supply of **glucose and oxygen** and must get rid of **carbon dioxide**. In animals, the **digestive system** provides glucose, the **lungs** provide oxygen, and the **circulatory system** delivers both to cells and carries away carbon dioxide. In plants, glucose is made by photosynthesis and oxygen diffuses in through the **stomata**.

bullets: Photosynthesis is **endothermic** (takes in energy from light); respiration is **exothermic** (releases energy).
Photosynthesis happens only in cells with **chloroplasts** in the light; respiration happens in **all living cells all the time**.
At the **compensation point**, the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration, so there is no net gas exchange (a common data question).
In the dark, plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide just like animals.
Plants make more glucose by photosynthesis than they use in respiration during the day, which is why they can grow.
Global link: deforestation and burning fossil fuels disturb this balance and increase atmospheric carbon dioxide.
core.p: Photosynthesis and respiration are **opposite processes**. Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen, while respiration uses glucose and oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water. The products of each are the reactants of the other. This gives a cycle that keeps the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere roughly balanced.

bullets: Test for CO2: limewater goes from **clear to cloudy/milky**.
Hydrogencarbonate indicator: **red** (atmospheric CO2) to **yellow** (more CO2) to **purple** (less CO2).
Germinating peas in a vacuum flask: thermometer reading rises because respiration is exothermic.
**Control**: use boiled and disinfected peas (killed, so no respiration) in an identical flask. This shows the temperature rise is due to living respiration and not the room.
**Disinfectant** prevents microorganisms on the peas from respiring and affecting results.
Control variables: mass of peas, volume of flask, starting temperature, time, same thermometer.
core.p: You can show that respiration is happening by detecting its products or its energy release. **Limewater** turns **cloudy (milky)** when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it, and **hydrogencarbonate indicator** turns from **red/orange to yellow** when carbon dioxide concentration rises. Heat release from respiring organisms (e.g. germinating peas in a vacuum flask) can be measured with a **thermometer**. These are good ideas for 'plan an investigation' questions, though they are not one of the AQA required practicals.

bullets: Increasing temperature increases rate up to the optimum (about 37 degrees C in humans).
Above the optimum the enzyme active site changes shape (**denatured**) and the rate drops sharply.
More oxygen available means a higher rate of aerobic respiration, up to a limit set by enzyme number.
More active cells (e.g. exercising muscle) respire faster because they use ATP faster.
Germinating seeds respire quickly because they are growing rapidly and need a lot of energy.
Graph skill: a rate against temperature graph rises, peaks at the optimum, then falls steeply.
core.h: Factors affecting the rate of respiration
core.p: Because respiration is controlled by enzymes, its rate depends on temperature, the availability of **glucose** and **oxygen**, and on how active the cell is. Warmer temperatures (up to the **optimum**) speed it up because particles move faster and collide more often, but very high temperatures **denature** the enzymes and respiration stops.

bullets: Warm-blooded animals (mammals, birds) respire faster because they use energy to maintain body temperature.
Small mammals have a high surface area to volume ratio, lose heat quickly and so respire faster per gram.
Cold-blooded animals respire more slowly in cold weather.
Seeds and bulbs respire slowly while dormant.
Yeast can respire aerobically when oxygen is present and anaerobically when it is not.
Link: the larger the organism, the greater the need for a transport system.
core.p: All living organisms respire, but how they obtain oxygen differs. Mammals breathe air into lungs, fish use gills, insects use tubes called tracheae, and plants use diffusion through stomata and lenticels. In every case the final process in the cells is the same equation. Single-celled organisms take in oxygen directly by diffusion across their cell membrane.

bullets: Mr of carbon dioxide CO2 = 12 + (2 x 16) = **44**.
Moles = mass / Mr. So 90 g glucose = 90 / 180 = 0.5 mol.
The moles of CO2 produced = 6 x 0.5 = 3 mol, so mass = 3 x 44 = **132 g**.
Aerobic respiration is more **efficient** because the carbon in glucose is completely oxidised to CO2.
Do not claim a precise number of ATP at GCSE unless the question gives it.
core.h: Higher tier extension: calculations and efficiency
core.p: At Higher tier you may be asked to use the symbol equation quantitatively or to compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration. In the equation the ratio of **moles** is 1 glucose : 6 oxygen : 6 carbon dioxide : 6 water. You can use relative formula masses (Mr) to work out masses. Aerobic respiration transfers **much more energy per glucose** than anaerobic respiration because the glucose is completely oxidised.

exam: 1 mark 'State the word equation for aerobic respiration': glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Reactants left, products right, arrow in the correct direction.
'Give the balanced symbol equation' (usually 2 marks): C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O. Marks for correct formulae and then for balancing.
'Describe' means give features or steps without reasons; 'explain' needs a reason using 'because'. Always use the word **'transfers energy'**.
For 'why do muscle cells contain many mitochondria?' (2 marks): mitochondria are where **aerobic respiration** takes place / most reactions happen; muscles need a lot of **energy** for contraction.
For 'why does respiration increase during exercise?' (3 marks): muscles contract more; more energy needed; more glucose and oxygen used; more carbon dioxide produced.
Three uses of energy: **build larger molecules**, **movement**, **keep warm**. Learn these exact three for a 3 mark list question.
Investigation questions: always include a **control** (e.g. boiled/dead peas), say what you will **measure** (temperature), and name **control variables**.
Data questions: describe the pattern first (as X increases, Y increases), quote figures with units, then explain using respiration.
6 mark questions: link several ideas in order: reactants, process in mitochondria, products, energy transferred, uses of energy, and comparison with anaerobic.
Higher tier: use Mr values only if given; state the formula you use (moles = mass / Mr), show each step and units.

mistakes.r: Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that transfers energy from glucose. Breathing is ventilation of the lungs.
mistakes.w: Respiration is breathing in and out.

mistakes.r: Energy cannot be made. Respiration transfers (releases) energy from glucose.
Plants respire all the time in all living cells; they photosynthesise only in the light.
mistakes.w: Plants only photosynthesise and do not respire.

mistakes.r: It is continuous in all living cells, even during sleep.
mistakes.w: Respiration only happens when we exercise.

mistakes.r: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Energy is transferred but is not a chemical product.
mistakes.w: Equation written as glucose + oxygen to energy.

mistakes.r: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O, with the same number of each atom on both sides.
mistakes.w: Writing the oxygen as O in the symbol equation or leaving it unbalanced.

mistakes.r: Respiration is exothermic: it transfers energy to the surroundings.
Mitochondria are the site of most of the reactions in aerobic respiration, which transfers energy.
mistakes.w: Mitochondria make energy / are the powerhouse that creates energy.

mistakes.r: All living cells respire continuously; the rate depends on temperature, activity and size.
mistakes.w: Cold-blooded or small animals have no need to respire fast.

summary: The specification requires you to know that respiration is an exothermic reaction that occurs continuously in all living cells, that aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose, and that you can recall the word and symbol equation for it. It matters because every living process (movement, building molecules, keeping warm) depends on the energy it transfers, and it links to photosynthesis, the circulatory system and exercise.

terms.d: An exothermic reaction that occurs continuously in living cells to transfer energy from glucose.
Respiration that uses oxygen to break down glucose completely, transferring a large amount of energy.
Respiration without oxygen, which transfers much less energy per glucose.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, usually shown by a temperature rise.
A simple sugar, C6H12O6, the main respiratory substrate in cells.
Sub-cellular structures where most of the reactions in aerobic respiration take place.
A substance that is used up in a chemical reaction (glucose and oxygen in respiration).
A substance made in a chemical reaction (carbon dioxide and water in aerobic respiration).
A solution that turns cloudy when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.
The light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration.
A biological catalyst, a protein that speeds up a reaction; respiration is controlled by enzymes.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
A comparison set up in the same way as the experiment but without the factor being tested, to show the effect is due to that factor.
Ventilation: moving air in and out of the lungs. It is not respiration.

worked.ans: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O (C 6, H 12, O 18 on both sides).
worked.q: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration and show that it is balanced. (3 marks)
steps: Glucose is C6H12O6, oxygen is O2, carbon dioxide is CO2, water is H2O.
Count right: C = 6; H = 6 x 2 = 12; O = 12 + 6 = 18.
Both sides equal so it is balanced.

worked.q: 90 g of glucose is respired aerobically. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced. (Relative atomic masses: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16) (4 marks, Higher)
steps: Equation ratio 1 glucose : 6 CO2, so moles CO2 = 0.5 x 6 = 3 mol.

worked.ans: The germinating peas in A are respiring (aerobic respiration), which is an exothermic reaction transferring energy as heat, so A is warmer. The boiled peas in B are dead so there is no respiration and no temperature rise; B is the control.
worked.q: A student puts germinating peas in a flask with a thermometer and boiled peas in an identical flask. After 24 hours flask A is 6 degrees C warmer than flask B. Explain the result. (3 marks)
steps: Say what is happening in A: living peas carry out aerobic respiration.
Link to the evidence: respiration is exothermic, so energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat.
Explain the control: boiled peas are dead so cannot respire, so B shows the temperature rise is not due to the room.
